title: The Shroud of Turin
hook: Why does a linen cloth baffle scientists for centuries?
headline: The relic that defies science

beats.label: THE CASE
beats.line: The shroud, a 14-foot linen bearing a 1988 carbon test, surfaced in Turin.

beats.label: CLUE 1
beats.line: In 1354, Pope Clement VII transferred the cloth to the Cathedral of Saint John.

beats.label: CLUE 2
beats.line: Scientists in 1978 photographed the shroud with a high-resolution camera, revealing faint blood patterns.

beats.label: THE TWIST
beats.line: A 2020 study claimed a natural chemical reaction formed the image, but experts disagree.

end.line: What do you think caused the mysterious image?

description: Explore the centuries-old mystery of the Shroud of Turin and its puzzling origins.

facts.claim: The shroud measures about 14.3 feet long and 3.5 feet wide.
Radiocarbon dating performed in 1988 dated the linen to the medieval period.
Pope Clement VII transferred the shroud to Turin in 1354.
In 1978, a high-resolution photograph captured faint bloodstains on the shroud.
A 2020 study suggested the image could result from a natural chemical reaction.
facts.source: Nature Communications, 2020 article on Shroud image formation

bad: contradicted: In 1354 Pope Clement VII transferred the cloth to the Cathedral of Saint John (spravne: No record of such a transfer; Pope Clement VII (antipope) wrote about the shroud in 1390, and the cloth was not transferred in 1354)

contradicted: Scientists in 1978 photographed the shroud with a high-resolution camera, revealing faint blood patterns (spravne: No high-resolution photograph was taken in 1978; the first photographs were made by Secondo Pia in 1898)
unsupported: The shroud is a 14-foot linen bearing a 1988 carbon test
unsupported: A 2020 study claimed a natural chemical reaction formed the image, but experts disagree
